intro: Averaging microbatch means equally gives small batches too much influence. Weight each mean gradient by its example count to recover the full-batch mean.
task: Combine microbatch mean gradients using example counts and demonstrate the bias from equally weighting unequal batches.
requirements: mean_gradients is a finite numeric array shaped (B,...) with B>0 and at least one parameter axis. sample_counts is a length-B vector of positive integer-valued counts at most 1000000.
Return a NumPy array shaped (...) equal to sum(count_i*gradient_i)/sum(count_i). The supplied gradients are means over each microbatch.
Do not divide by the number of microbatches after sample weighting. No optimizer step or autograd engine is part of this operation.

Numeric inputs must be real and finite with magnitude at most 1e30, except where a stricter bound is stated. Booleans are not numeric parameters. Leave all caller inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Recover sums before averaging
hints.body: A mean gradient multiplied by its example count becomes a summed gradient.

hints.title: Broadcast weights over parameters
hints.body: Only the leading axis indexes microbatches; every remaining axis belongs to parameters.

explanation: The full-batch mean is a sample-weighted combination of microbatch means. Equal averaging is correct only when microbatches have equal example counts.

This is an algebraic accumulation lesson with supplied gradients. Stateful layers, stochastic masks, and loss normalization can make actual microbatch training differ from a single large-batch forward pass.
